BetterGov Fellowship 2026 · Energy challenge

One open energy data layer

This is my proposal for the Energy challenge set by the Department of Energy with the Mura, Malinis, at Maaasahang Kuryente Coalition. Everything else on this site is the prototype I built for it.

The problem

In June 2026 the average residential rate in the Philippines was ₱12.43/kWh, the highest in ASEAN, and off-grid it reached ₱24.92. Yet no consumer or LGU can compare its utility against the rest.

DOE already compiles monthly rates for {{utilities}} distribution utilities, but by hand, in a spreadsheet with no stable IDs, where {{nda_share}} of the cells say "no data". Suppliers, utilities and electric cooperatives sit in ERC, DOE and NEA records with no common ID. Each utility publishes its rates in its own way (PDFs, web tables, Facebook posts), and someone has to copy them in every month.

What I'll build

I want to build one open energy data layer around DOE's three asks.

The first is a master list of suppliers, distribution utilities and cooperatives. Each one gets a stable code, keeps its source IDs from ERC, DOE and NEA, and carries its franchise area as PSGC codes, so every province, city and barangay can be joined to the utility that serves it. The list is published as an API.

The second is a monthly price table: utility, month, customer class, price per kWh and generation charge. It starts from DOE's compiled sheet. Scrapers and parsers then read each utility's own rate notices, fill the gaps, and flag where the two disagree. Every row links to its source, and the coalition's analyst checks it before release.

The third is the set of feeds behind DOE's renewable-energy and priority-project dashboards, so they update from source and anyone can download the data behind them. If ERC agrees, I'd also parse its monthly generation-charge filings. Consumers, LGUs, researchers and the coalition would use all of it through a "your utility, your price" view and the API.

What the prototype found

Before applying, I wanted to know whether this holds up against the real data, so I built the prototype on this site. It turns DOE's sheet into an open dataset for all {{utilities}} utilities, {{first_month}} to {{latest_month}}, gives each one a stable ID, and maps {{with_prov}} franchise areas to PSGC codes. Then it reads {{n_checked}} utilities' own rate documents, PDFs and images both, and lines them up against DOE's numbers. These are the first results.

The gaps can be filled. {{fill_sentence}} Each filled cell keeps the document it came from, and is listed in filled.csv and on the source checks page.

DOE's generation charges hold up; its residential rates need a stated method. Every generation charge I could check matches DOE's entry. The differences are all residential rates: {{diff_list}}. Part of that is which consumption level DOE reads off a bill. In {{meralco_level_n}} Meralco months from 2018 and 2019, DOE's figure is exactly Meralco's own {{meralco_level}} kWh bill, while since {{meralco_200_from}} it has been the 200 kWh bill. DOE doesn't publish which level it uses, so I treat the rest as questions to ask, and each one sits on the source checks page with the utility's document open beside it.

The sheet has its own problems. The pipeline found {{issues_total}} entries that can't be right as typed, among them negative rates, a ₱6,447/kWh commercial rate, and a date typed where a rate should be, plus rows where the sheet's tabs disagree about the same utility.

The hardest part is reaching every utility. DOE's sheet links {{links_fb}} utilities only to a Facebook page, and {{links_bad}} of the websites it links to didn't load when I checked. Meta doesn't allow automated reading without its permission, so part of the work is getting those notices to DOE in a form a machine can read. How I'd get there is in the methodology.

How it connects to DBM COMPASS

PSGC is the join key COMPASS already uses for local governments, so every LGU page in COMPASS could show its power provider and what it charges.

The open API is described in OpenAPI 3.1, and the downloads carry Frictionless and DCAT metadata, which covers data.gov.ph. An MCP server will cover COMPASS's MCP-compatible integrations. Where DOE requires it, field names will follow ASEAN Energy Statistics conventions. You can try the prototype's version of the API on the Data & API page.

December to March
  1. December List the sources, build master list v0 from the prototype, and agree the schema with DOE and the coalition's analyst.
  2. January Scrapers for the first batch of utilities, price table v1 with discrepancy reports, and the API.
  3. February Cover as many of the {{utilities}} utilities as publish online, add the DOE dashboard feeds, and add the consumer view.
  4. March Documentation, a maintenance runbook for the scrapers, and Demo Day.
What I've built before

As a BetterGov volunteer, I rebuilt the FY2027 House budget bill (₱3.86 trillion as filed) from its PDFs into open, joinable tables, with official UACS and PSGC codes and every printed total kept so each line can be checked. It's the same approach as this prototype, and it's on GitHub.

I also lead the Naga City People's Budget Portal (budget.naga.gov.ph) as CTO of Stride Technologies. Since October 2026 it has published the city's 2027 investment program (332 programs, ₱8.13B), and every figure has to match the city's documents to the centavo. The same approach now covers other cities: the portal's LGU budget comparison takes the enacted budgets of Naga, Zamboanga and Cagayan de Oro out of their PDFs and puts them side by side, by expense class, by office and over the years, with every figure traceable to its source.
